blocks.text: The figure of the eagle upon its throne, and the council of birds sitting around it. That is, in the council of the birds the eagle is depicted, distinguished by a crown and raised high on a throne, and the other birds stand by it. And of the eagle Baal Hatturim says, right at the beginning of this chapter, הוא מלך העופות, It holds kingship over the birds. Finally, the Fathers define the very same thing. Thus Ambrose, Hexaëm. book 5, ch. 18, calls the eagle a royal bird and attributes to it royal eminence. Jerome on Mich. 1: The eagle, which is queen of the birds. And on Dan. VII.: As the lion holds kingship among the beasts, so the eagle among the birds. Epiphanius in the Physiologus, chapter 6: Ἔστι γὰρ ὁ ἀετὸς βασιλεὺς τῶν ὀρνέων· [Esti gar ho aetos basileus tōn orneōn] For the eagle is king of the birds, or queen, if you prefer. Theodoret, in the Preface to the Song, on the passage Ezech. XVII, 3.: Ἀετὸν μὲν τὸν βασιλέα (ἐνόησεν), ἐπειδὰν καὶ τὸ ζῶον βασιλικόν· [Aeton men ton basilea (enoēsen), epeidan kai to zōon basilikon] By the name of eagle he meant the king, because it is a royal animal. Theodore of Heraclea on Psal. CII.: Ἐπειδὴ ὁ ἀετὸς δοκεῖ βασιλεύειν τῶν πετεινῶν ἁπάντων· [Epeidē ho aetos dokei basileuein tōn peteinōn hapantōn] Because the eagle seems to rule over all the birds. And a little later: Διὰ γὰρ τοῦ ὄρνιθος τοῦ ἀετοῦ τὴν βασιλείαν αἰνίττεται, [Dia gar tou ornithos tou aetou tēn basileian ainittetai] For by the eagle he signifies the kingdom. What of the fact that it was commonly believed that the eagle is at war with the wren because the latter καλεῖται πρέσβυς, καὶ βασιλεὺς [kaleitai presbys, kai basileus], is called senator and king, as though it begrudged it this name? So the Philosopher attests, Hist. book 9, ch. 11. Hence Pliny, book 10, ch. 74: The eagle and the wren are at odds, if we believe it, because the latter is called king of the birds.

Whence the eagle, in Hebrew נשר neser, gets its name has so far escaped the masters. For absurd is the fancy of Rabbi Bechai on Gen. II. that it derives from the Chaldee נשר nesar, which means to fall down, because, after it has risen in flight to the element of fire, as they indeed would have it, it then falls headlong into the sea. Nor do I agree with those who assert that it is named from the shedding of its feathers, because נשר among the Rabbis means to fall off; or from sight, because נשר neser seems to allude to the verb שור sur, which means to see. Rather, I most approve of the Arabs, for whom نسر [nasara] nasara means to pluck with the beak, and منسر [minsar] minsar means beak, and properly that of a bird of prey. From this, then, they hold that the eagle is called نسر [nasr] nesr, لانه ينسر الشي ويقتلعه [li-annahu yansiru al-shay wa-yaqtaliʿuhu] because it tears and plucks a thing with its beak. So Giauhari, Damir and Alcamus. Other birds of prey also pluck with the beak; yet this is ascribed by special right to the prince of the birds of prey, the eagle, [col. 165] because its beak is more hooked and it tears more forcefully with it. Likewise, swooping upon prey is common to all, which in Hebrew is העיט. Hence עיט ajit is in general [II, 743] a bird of prey. Yet usage among the Greeks made ἀετόν [aeton] or αἰετόν [aieton], derived from it, the proper name of the eagle ^{(1)}.

The eagle is remarkable not only for its beak but also for its talons, which it has not straight, like a man, but curved and hooked like a lion's. For of the animals that have claws, τὰ μέν εἰσιν εὐθυόνυχα, ὥσπερ ἄνθρωπος· τὰ δὲ γαμψώνυχα, ὥσπερ καὶ τῶν πεζῶν λέων, καὶ τῶν πτηνῶν αἰετὸς [ta men eisin euthyonycha, hōsper anthrōpos; ta de gampsōnycha, hōsper kai tōn pezōn leōn, kai tōn ptēnōn aietos], some have straight claws, like man; others hooked, like the lion among land animals and the eagle among birds. So the Philosopher, Hist. book 3, ch. 9. In birds, that is, the talons imitate the shape of the beak. Suidas: Γαμψώνυχα ὅσα τῶν ζώων τὴν ἐπιρυγχίδα γεγάμψωκεν ὑπὸ τὴν γένυν, οἷα ἐστὶν ἀετός· [Gampsōnycha hosa tōn zōōn tēn epirynchida gegampsōken hypo tēn genyn, hoia estin aetos] Those animals have hooked claws which have a beak curved beneath the jaws, to which kind the eagle belongs. The Grammarians are uncertain to which of the two it refers that the eagle which the sleepless Penelope saw is called

For to some ἀγκυλοχείλης [ankylocheilēs] is ὁ ἔχων ἀγκύλα χείλη, ἤτοι τὸ ῥάμφος [ho echōn ankyla cheilē, ētoi to rhamphos], one that has curved lips, [II, 744] that is, a curved beak; to others ἐπικαμπεῖς τὰς χηλὰς ἔχων [epikampeis tas chēlas echōn], one that has bent talons. In this sense, in Aristophanes' Knights, Cleon is called
because like an eagle he had hooked or rapacious claws, as not only the Scholiast but also Aristophanes himself explains. And in Plautus' Pseudolus the cook says,
Do you expect to find any cook who has not a kite's or an eagle's talons?
